question:
We hold people responsible only for what lies within their control: this is among the least controversial of moral principles, and among the least honoured. Consider two drivers, equally careless, distracted for the same fraction of a second. One arrives home; the other kills a child who has stepped off the kerb. The law will treat them differently, and so will we - and so, most tellingly, will they treat themselves. The second driver's remorse is not merely more intense than the first's; it has a different object. He mourns what he did, not what he risked doing. Yet nothing in his agency, nothing he chose or willed, distinguishes him from the driver who got home.

The comfortable response is that our differing reactions are useful rather than just: outcomes are easy to observe, intentions are not, and a legal system that punished risk alone would be both intrusive and unworkable. But this concedes the point while pretending to answer it. It explains why we behave as if outcome mattered; it does not touch the second driver's conviction that he has become something the first has not. To tell him his guilt is an administrative convenience is to ask him to regard his own moral life as a misunderstanding.

Perhaps the principle itself is the error. It may be that agency was never the sealed inner chamber the principle imagines - that to act at all is to hand oneself over to a world which will finish one's actions in ways one cannot foresee, and that the self we are judged by is partly the world's handiwork. The principle does not so much fail as reveal that it was describing a creature we are not.

Which of the following best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: (a) The law errs in punishing outcomes rather than intentions, since only intention lies within an agent's control.
(b) Practical necessity justifies holding agents answerable for outcomes even though such accountability is strictly undeserved.
(c) The gap between the control principle and our actual moral responses indicates a defect not in the responses but in the conception of agency the principle assumes.
(d) Remorse is an unreliable guide to moral responsibility because it tracks consequences rather than choices.
explanation: The final paragraph relocates the error: not in our responses but in the principle itself, which 'was describing a creature we are not.' Closest wrong (b): this is the 'comfortable response' the passage says 'concedes the point while pretending to answer it' - a position rejected, not held.

The author's rejection of the "comfortable response" depends on the assumption that
options: (a) legal systems ought to track moral desert as closely as institutional design permits.
(b) an agent's own experience of guilt carries evidential weight about moral reality and cannot simply be explained away as a psychological artefact.
(c) careless driving is morally wrong whether or not it results in harm.
(d) punishing risk in the absence of harm would be impractical and intrusive.

Which one of the following can be most safely inferred from the passage?
options: (a) The author holds that the two drivers are, in the final analysis, equally blameworthy.
(b) The author regards the legal distinction drawn between the two drivers as arbitrary.
(c) The author holds that a moral principle should be abandoned whenever it conflicts with common intuition.
(d) The author treats the difference in the two drivers' self-assessments as data a theory of responsibility must accommodate rather than dismiss.

The author would most likely DISAGREE with which one of the following statements?
options: (a) Our harsher response to the unlucky driver is best understood as a socially useful fiction with no moral foundation.
(b) A person may become, through what happens, someone he had no intention of becoming.
(c) The claim that responsibility extends only to what we control enjoys wide assent.
(d) Moral self-assessment can outrun what the agent actually chose.

question:
Defenders of international law are fond of pointing out how much of it is obeyed. Treaties on postal routes, diplomatic immunity, maritime boundaries and civil aviation are honoured with a regularity that domestic criminal law might envy, and all this without a sheriff. From this the inference is drawn that law can bind without coercion, that obligation has a force of its own.

The inference is too quick. A rule that states would have followed anyway, because following it serves each of them, is not tested by their following it. Much of international law is of exactly this kind: it coordinates rather than constrains. It tells states which side of the road to drive on, and once the convention exists no one gains by departing from it. Compliance here is evidence of the rule's convenience, not of its authority. The interesting cases are those in which a state's interest and its obligation come apart - and it is precisely there that the record thins.

This is not a case for cynicism, only for asking a different question. The relevant measure of a legal order is not the volume of compliance but its behaviour under strain: whether obligations are invoked, whether departures must be justified in the law's own vocabulary rather than merely announced, whether the justification offered constrains what can be claimed next. A state that violates a norm while insisting it has done no such thing is paying the norm a peculiar kind of tribute - and, more to the point, is narrowing the ground on which it can stand when the next case arises. By that measure international law is neither the toothless thing its detractors describe nor the quiet success its defenders infer from the tally of treaties kept.

Which of the following best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: (a) International law is largely ineffective because it lacks centralised enforcement machinery.
(b) High rates of compliance are weak evidence of international law's authority; its strength is better judged by how obligations behave when interests pull against them.
(c) Since most international law merely coordinates state behaviour, it serves no genuinely constraining purpose.
(d) States that violate norms while denying the violation show that international law is enforced through reputational cost.
explanation: Paragraph two disarms the compliance argument; paragraph three proposes behaviour under strain as the substitute measure. Closest wrong (c): it overreaches - the passage says coordination rules do not demonstrate authority, not that law has no constraining purpose, and the closing line refuses the toothless verdict outright.

Which one of the following can be most safely inferred from the passage?
options: (a) A fall in the number of treaties in force would signal a weakening of the international legal order.
(b) Rules of diplomatic immunity are observed chiefly because breach would invite retaliation in kind.
(c) A norm whose violations are routinely accompanied by denials is doing more work than one that is simply never at issue.
(d) The author believes treaties on technical matters ought not to be classified as law at all.

The tone of the passage is best described as
options: (a) sceptical and dismissive
(b) detached and non-committal
(c) indignant and reformist
(d) discriminating and measured
explanation: The author draws a careful distinction, corrects one side, then refuses the opposite conclusion - 'neither the toothless thing... nor the quiet success.' Closest wrong (b): the analysis is cool, but 'this is not a case for cynicism' and the proposed measure are commitments, so the author is not non-committal.

(b) The absence of a central enforcer renders the very concept of international law incoherent.
(c) A state's need to cast its conduct in legal terms is itself a form of constraint.
